View code
import polars as pl
from plotnine import ggplot, aes
from polars import col as c

import funs

ub = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/taylor-arnold/fds2/refs/heads/main/"




View code
film = (
    pl.read_csv(ub + "data/criterion.csv")
    .select(
        c.title, c.year, c.director, c.country, c.language, c.genre,
        c.runtime_raw, c.imdb_votes, c.rating_imdb, c.rating_rt, c.rating_mc
    )
    .drop_nulls(subset=["runtime_raw", "imdb_votes", "rating_imdb"])
)




Questions
The film dataset describes the films released by the Criterion Collection, a distribution company that publishes restored editions of films it considers important. Each row is one film, with its title, year of release, director, country of production, language, and genre, along with its runtime_raw (in minutes) and three critical scores: rating_imdb (0-10), rating_rt (Rotten Tomatoes, 0-100), and rating_mc (Metacritic, 0-100). The column imdb_votes records how many IMDb users rated the film, which is a rough measure of how widely seen it is.
Unless a question says otherwise, just print the result of each block; do not save it to a variable.

Start by sorting the films by year, with the oldest films at the top.



View code
(
    film
    .sort(c.year)
)

Our dataset actually contains 198 films that Japan had a hand in producing, but the previous question found only 172. Look closely at the values in the country column. Why does our filter miss the other 26 films?

Answer: Films with more than one production country store all of them in a single value, separated by a vertical bar: "Japan|France", "Japan|United States", and so on. The test c.country == "Japan" asks whether the whole value is exactly the four letters Japan, so a co-production like "Japan|France" answers False and is dropped. Data stored this way is annoying to work with, and we will see how to split it apart later in the semester.

The order of the first two methods matters here. .drop_nulls() looks at every column it is given, so calling it on the whole dataset would also throw away films that are missing only a Rotten Tomatoes score, even though we never asked about Rotten Tomatoes. Narrowing to the three columns we care about first keeps the method from removing more than we intended.

import polars as pl
from plotnine import ggplot, aes
from polars import col as c

import funs

ub = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/taylor-arnold/fds2/refs/heads/main/"




Questions
Welcome to the first notebook. The goal today is just to get comfortable running code, so every question is short. Each gray box is a code cell: click into it and press Shift+Enter to run it. The result shows up right below. To see the result of something, type it into a cell and run it.
We will start by using Python as a calculator, then create a few variables, and finish with our first function.

Add the numbers 8 and 15.



View code
8 + 15


23



There are 24 hours in a day. Multiply to find how many hours are in a week of 7 days.



View code
24 * 7


168



Python follows the usual order of operations, and parentheses let you control it. Run the expression below and check that the answer is what you expected.



View code
(20 - 5) / 3


5.0



Instead of just looking at a result, we can store it. Create a variable named mynum that holds the value of 3 + 5.



View code
mynum = 3 + 5



Nothing appeared below the cell in the previous question. Why not?

Answer: The result was saved into the variable mynum instead of being displayed. Storing a value and showing a value are two different things: an assignment with = keeps the result for later but does not print it.

Now use your variable. Add 1 to mynum.



View code
